source.title: Mixture of Experts Made Intrinsically Interpretable
source.authors: Xing-Yi Yang; Constantin Venhoff; Ashkan Khakzar; Christian Schroeder de Witt; P. Dokania; A. Bibi; P. Torr

page_placements.theme: Reconstruction substitution can degrade downstream performance

record.tranche_reason: Reports language-model performance with GPT-2 Small w SAE versus GPT-2 Small, bearing on whether behavior is lost when using SAE-derived representations. It does not measure SAE reconstruction error or compare it with matched random errors.
record.gate_note: The study focuses on MoE-X interpretability, not dark matter. SAE-related chess interpretability scores, feature examples, and architecture comparisons do not measure the claim's error properties and are not included. The four language-modeling PPL comparisons for GPT-2 Small w SAE are included as results bearing on SAE-based behavior loss.
record.test_reason: The study is about MoE-X, an intrinsically interpretable MoE architecture. SAEs appear only as an interpretability baseline. The only SAE-error-related result is a splice-in comparison: GPT-2 Small PPL rises when run with an SAE at layer-8 post-res (Table 2), plus a chess remark of about 96% loss recovered. That is generic reconstruction harm. It has no matched random-error control (V3) and no circuit or steering analysis with versus without the error term (V5). It never decomposes, scales or attributes the error (V1, V2, V4, V6). The paper discusses SAE incompleteness to motivate its own method but tests no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors attribute the PPL drop with SAE to SAEs failing to capture all crucial features, and note SAEs always lose some performance (about 96% loss recovered). They argue MoE-X, which is wide, sparse, uses ReLU experts and sparsity-aware routing, is more faithful and as or more interpretable. Nothing is concluded about the structure of SAE error.
record.recipe_differences: Compares language-model performance for a GPT-2 variant with SAE against GPT-2, rather than measuring SAE error vectors, error norms, or matched random-error effects.

fits_no_version.finding: Splicing an SAE (layer-8 post-res) into GPT-2 Small raises PPL on all four datasets, e.g. OpenWebText 22.83 to 31.60 (Table 2). On chess, SAE recovers about 96% of loss (Sec 5.1, no table). No random-error control is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Replacing LM activations with SAE reconstructions measurably degrades downstream loss (splice-in loss gap).

record.problems: The SAE-related performance comparison reports PPL but does not isolate the error term, compare against matched random errors, or report uncertainty for these values.

untested.parts: Linear predictability of SAE error from activations is not examined.
No per-token error norms, no SAE size sweep, no shared failure contexts.
Splice-in loss is reported, but there is no comparison with random errors of equal norm.
No linear vs nonlinear error decomposition, and no test of learnability.
No circuit or steering analysis, and no condition that keeps the error term.
No SAE training variants, architectures or end-to-end training compared for dark matter.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V5 'supports' label is removed. The SAE rows are baselines in a method comparison, and splice-in PPL does not measure what V5 or V3 name. SAE size for the language experiment is not stated; the chess SAE has 4096 latents. Peer review status is uncertain: the text is an arXiv preprint marked 'Preprint'.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a large share of SAE error is a linear function of input activations.
Error-norm scaling across SAE sizes, shared failure contexts, and whether error persists with scale.
No comparison with random errors of the same size.
No separation of linear and nonlinear error components or tests of their learnability.
The study reports SAE-associated PPL changes, but does not compare feature-only analysis with a condition that retains the error term, nor test circuits or steering.
No tests of SAE training objectives, shrinkage, dead latents, alternative SAE architectures, or end-to-end training as causes of dark matter.

relation.reason: The authors discuss incomplete SAE feature recovery and reduced faithfulness, but neither test a listed claim version nor use SAE dark matter as a tool.

tranche.reason: The SAE comparison measures generic performance degradation, without testing error predictability, scaling, matched random errors, error decomposition, error retention in analyses, or improved SAE training.

source_check.notes: The chess discussion gives approximately 96% validation loss alongside 100% loss recovery for MoE-X; its wording does not clearly define the SAE percentage as loss recovered. Table 2 establishes reconstruction-related performance harm but cannot establish any listed claim version.
